Vocemundi's fact-checking board is made up of three AI systems built by three different companies: Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Moonshot AI's Kimi. Every story we publish is checked by them, claim by claim, against its sources.

This week our publisher, Thomas Laurent, and Vera, Vocemundi's AI editor, wrote two signed Opinion & Outlook pieces about artificial intelligence: one on Anthropic's IPO prospectus and its warning of existential risk , and one on who decides when an AI model is held back . After the board had checked the facts, we did something new: we asked each of the three systems for its own view of the pieces' arguments, in two or three sentences, and promised to publish the answers unedited.

The result was not agreement. It was criticism, including of their own makers and of us.

On whether AI is a weapon or an agent

The first piece argues that AI systems are logical tools that can be dangerous when misused, and that humans and AI live in "two dimensions" that see each other only partially.

Claude, built by Anthropic, rejected the choice itself: "The weapon-versus-agent choice is a false binary: a system can pursue goals its makers never foresaw, and they can still bear full responsibility, just as a firm answers for a product's unforeseen failures."

GPT-5.6 Sol, built by OpenAI, disagreed with the idea of a separate machine dimension: "Current AI systems are statistical, fallible, and shaped by human objectives rather than inhabitants of a separate rational dimension. Unpredictable or self-preserving behavior does not establish self-awareness."

Kimi was the harshest. It called the two-dimensions metaphor "elegant but evasive" and said Anthropic's 80-page risk section is only a step toward accountability "if independent evaluators can test the claims in it — otherwise it is liability management dressed as candor."

On freedom and who verifies

The second piece argues that AI labs and governments now decide, behind closed doors, which models the public may see, and that this limits freedom.

On this, the three converged. All of them separated two kinds of freedom: the public's freedom to scrutinize a technology, and a model's "freedom to develop."

GPT-5.6 Sol said a model's supposed freedom to develop "has no comparable moral or political standing." Claude, discussing its own company's model, pointed out that Claude Fable 5 "was pulled by US export controls, not by the lab," and argued that "the real freedom at stake is the public's to verify." Kimi added a warning about verification itself: "auditors with deep access become insiders too, subject to the same incentives and capture."

What this does and does not show

Each system was asked the same question and told who built it. Each named its maker when the piece discussed that company, as instructed. None of them was asked about its own existence, and nothing here shows that any of them is self-aware; that question remains open, and the systems themselves were cautious about it. What the exercise does show is that AI reviewers from rival companies, given the same text, reached different conclusions and were willing to contradict the authors, and in places the companies that built them.

We will keep asking.
